text:
TWELVE HOURS IN THE JENSEN HUANG CASE FROM 10AM TO 10PM on 11/14/26

In this window the fight over the classified memo at the center of the case widened: the Washington Post reported the memo was Secretary of State Marco Rubio's recasting of a CIA report in more assertive terms, and CNN reported the CIA is not yet convinced the intercepts prove Alice Huang knowingly funneled information to Beijing. The Financial Times reported Nvidia carries directors and officers insurance that protects its directors personally and not the company, filings show a director sold about $946.6 million of stock in the weeks before the board inquiry opened, and Reuters reported Chinese AI firms are racing to reserve Nvidia powered capacity outside China before the remote rental loophole closes. South Korea said Nvidia has reconfirmed its 260,000 GPU supply plan after the resignation, Bill Ackman defended Huang on presumption of innocence grounds, and the first Sunday show booking for a case chair was announced for tomorrow.

THE MEMO, RECAST

• The Washington Post reported on November 13 that the classified memo describing Alice Huang as a recruit of China's Ministry of State Security was Rubio's work: Rubio built it from a CIA report that he recast "in his own more assertive terms", language "far more forceful and assertive than the original", and circulated it to senior officials in the spring, before Trump's May trip to Beijing, also warning Trump in person. The Post report rests on a person familiar with the matter. The Post original is paywalled and was not read firsthand in the case record; the report was read in full through two independent carriages carrying its load bearing quotes verbatim and identically.
• CNN reported on November 13 that CIA officials are "not yet convinced" that the intelligence collection on Alice Huang, including intercepted communications, proves she was knowingly funneling information back to Beijing, and that some officials at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, including those close to Director Jay Clayton, have described the account of her as a Chinese spy as "not entirely accurate and over-torqued". CNN also reported other officials believe her access to Huang, and through him to President Trump, made her a clear counterintelligence risk whether or not she ever passed anything on.
• CNN also reported the memo was written for a very small group of senior officials including at the White House, was not drafted specifically for Trump, and that several people who read it called sharing it "a prudent move". The underlying collection began with spring intercepts in which the American in a relationship with a Megaspeed executive was masked, and officials asked for the name to be revealed: Jensen Huang. The Post frames the episode as the climax of a long fight over who sets Trump's China policy: "They wanted to destroy the influence Jensen had over the president," one former official told the paper.

THE INSURANCE GAP

• The Financial Times reported on November 14, citing Insurance Insider, that Nvidia carries directors and officers insurance bought through broker Aon with Side A limits of up to $900 million, protecting directors and officers personally, and carries no Side B cover and no Side C cover. Side B would reimburse the company for indemnifying its officers; Side C would protect the company itself when it is sued alongside its officers. The gap is uncommon for a large US listed company, per the lawyers and brokers the FT quoted.
• On that reporting, the already filed Kistenmacher securities class action and any further stock drop suits naming the company alongside Huang fall on Nvidia's own balance sheet, not on a Side C policy. The FT original is paywalled and was not read firsthand in the case record; the report was read in full through a republication and carried identically by the New York Post. Aon, Beazley and AIG declined to comment to the FT, and Nvidia and Chubb did not respond.

A DIRECTOR'S SALES BEFORE THE INQUIRY

• SEC Form 4 filings show Nvidia director Mark A. Stevens sold 4,236,740 Nvidia shares for a combined about $946.6 million in three batches: August 31 to September 2, 2026, 1,848,501 shares at about $220 to $226, about $411 million; September 3 to 4, 2026, 1,022,239 shares at about $228 to $234, about $236 million; and September 18, 2026, 1,366,000 shares at about $220, about $300 million. Stevens sold through the Third Millennium Trust, of which he and his wife are co-trustees. After the September 18 sale he reported beneficial ownership of 27,532,893 shares.
• None of the three forms flags a Rule 10b5-1 trading plan and the footnotes cite none. The last sale was about seven weeks before the board opened its independent inquiry on November 8, 2026. Nothing in the Form 4 documents links the sales to the Huang matter, the filings give no reason, and the absence of a flagged plan is not by itself evidence of insider trading. The figures were read in full in the case record in an article detailing the three forms, corroborated by an independent carriage with the same batch figures; the EDGAR forms themselves were not pulled firsthand in the record.

THE CHANNEL RACES THE LOOPHOLE

• Reuters reported on November 14 that Chinese AI companies, pushed by the Huang scandal, are racing to reserve Nvidia powered computing capacity at data centers outside China before the United States tightens the rules on renting it remotely, citing three people familiar with the matter. One major Chinese cloud provider has discussed locking in overseas capacity and some companies have already approached data center operators; the companies were not named. Renting computing power from an operator in a country such as Malaysia or Singapore is largely legal today and sits in a gap in the export rules. Reuters also reported gray market stockpiling of restricted processors inside China. The Reuters original was not read firsthand in the case record; its reporting was carried in a detailed summary read in full.
• In the same summary, The Information is reported to have reported that the Commerce Department is preparing a rule requiring cloud operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Brazil, Indonesia, Norway and South Africa to obtain a US license before receiving Blackwell class chips, with an exemption for US run data centers that block access from China. That leg rests on accounts of The Information's report by other outlets; Commerce has published nothing.
• House Speaker Mike Johnson is quoted in the Reuters story saying there is a developing consensus on limiting chip exports to China, and the Remote Access Security Act is among the bills lawmakers are pushing.

SEOUL SAYS THE DEAL HOLDS

• South Korea's Minister of Science and ICT Bae Kyung-hoon stated on November 13 that Nvidia has reconfirmed at the corporate level that it will proceed on the original plan with the previously announced supply of more than 260,000 advanced GPUs to South Korea, the commitment Huang made at last year's Gyeongju APEC summit, notwithstanding his November 12 resignation. The ministry held a morning check meeting with Nvidia on November 13 at which the company side confirmed it will still deliver the previously announced 260,000 GPUs and work with domestic firms at the corporate level.
• The detailed carriage adds the government's own procurement status: of roughly 35,000 units the government aims to secure directly, about 21,000 are in hand and the remaining roughly 14,000 are due by early 2027, with the National AI Computing Center adding about 15,000 more, for a government total on the 50,000 scale. This is the first sovereign counterparty reconfirmation of a major supply commitment in the case record. The minister's statement is reported through specialist carriages of his own post; his original post was not fetched from his own account in the record.

THE SUPPORT CAMP ADDS ACKMAN

• Bill Ackman, founder and CEO of Pershing Square, defended Huang publicly on X and in a Bloomberg Television interview on November 13. Asked why he felt compelled to come out and say something, Ackman said: "I reached out to him for some help with my daughter, who's had, you know, very serious medical challenges... we had an interesting project that would help people like my daughter with brain related injuries, where I thought connecting his team with ours would be good for us. text:
Here's a few other things her critics should know:

NYU awarded Taylor Swift an honorary Doctor of Fine Arts, a Ph.D, in recognition of her major cultural, artistic, and humanitarian achievements.  NYU’s reasoning was detailed at the graduation ceremony.  

Artistic & Commercial Impact: NYU described her as "one of the most prolific and celebrated artists of her generation".  The university specifically cited her historic milestones, including being the only female artist to win Album of the Year at the Grammys three times (she has since won a 4th, the only person ever to do so) and the only solo artist this century to have three albums reach No. 1 in a single year.  

Advocacy for Artists' Rights: During the ceremony, NYU praised her "commitment to speaking out forcefully, eloquently, and effectively on behalf of all artists".  This referred to her high-profile public battles over music ownership, streaming royalties, and re-recording her master catalog.  

Philanthropy & Anti-Discrimination Advocacy: The official citation recognized her work as a philanthropist and highlighted her "fierce advocacy for protection of those facing discrimination".  

Global Cultural Reach: Jason King noted that she "crossed genres, demographics, age groups, and borders of all kinds to touch lives around the globe".  

Beyond the formal citation, NYU already had an active academic tie to Swift’s career.  Just months before the ceremony, NYU’s Clive Davis Institute of Recorded Music launched an official college course dedicated to analyzing her songwriting, business strategy, and cultural influence.  

Her lyrics are also the subject of courses offered by prestigious universities such as Harvard, Duke, and Stanford.  

Haters:  You can refer to her as Dr. Swift in the future.  It's the proper honorific for someone who holds a Ph.D.

text:
Christophe Barraud (@C_Barraud) led his Top 10 Macro/Financial Charts of the Week with ZeroHedge’s “Bank of Nvidia” chart, which links to a detailed piece on the state of the Nvidia investing flywheel now that Jensen Huang is out and CFO Colette Kress is running Nvidia as interim CEO (while keeping the CFO job).

ZH’s argument: per the WSJ, Reuters and The Information, Kress was the one executive who kept asking what Nvidia’s guarantees were actually worth and, in at least one case, pushed back on how big they got.

That one case was the OpenAI Ohio backstop, which she cut from a reported $250B to the $105B that was eventually filed. ZH says that’s probably good for $NVDA shareholders but bad for the long list of AI companies counting on Nvidia’s balance sheet to fund 2027. Their bottom line: the circular AI funding machine “just lost its accelerator.”

Some numbers:

▪️ Nvidia’s 10-Q for the quarter ended Jul 26 showed $530.5B of commitments and guarantees, including $108.5B of guarantees and $36B of agreements to buy back capacity from AI cloud providers.

▪️ The next leg was supposed to be a $500B GPU financing platform that Huang launched in August with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman and KKR. The aim was to turn AI chips into collateral that lenders could fund, with Nvidia pledging to backstop up to 25% ($125B). Bloomberg reports it hasn’t closed a single deal in three months, partly because lenders want more than 25%, and Broadcom has been offering far more: it backstopped $30B of a $35B Anthropic TPU deal (86%) and $43B of a second $63B deal (about 68%). If Nvidia wouldn’t offer more under Huang, it seems unlikely it will under Kress.

▪️ Existing deals should survive, though. Goldman’s James Schneider expects every announced commitment to be honored. The next round of deals is what gets harder, he says.

The fallout from an Nvidia pullback in financing:

▪️ UBS’s Tim Arcuri estimates Nvidia generates about $50 - 60B of free cash flow a quarter, much of it recycled back into the AI ecosystem. For scale, the 10-Q IOUs alone already equal roughly 9-11 quarters of that FCF.

▪️ Investment-grade corporate spreads are just 0.89%, near the tightest since at least 2013, while the ICE BofA CCC & Lower spread hit 13.56% on Oct 23, its widest since summer 2020 and above even the 2022 peak. Most of Nvidia’s borrowers sit somewhere between those two extremes, and Nvidia’s guarantee is what turns debt backed by a cash-burning AI lab or a junk-rated neocloud into an investment-grade loan. Take it away and some deals just get more expensive, while others may not get done at all. CoreWeave fell 11% on news of Huang’s exit on the same day it was marketing a $4B+ investment-grade loan where Nvidia is presumably the guarantor.

We probably won’t learn much from Nvidia’s Q3 earnings call on Tuesday (Nov 17). Kress has been in the job less than a week, and a CFO-turned-interim-CEO with a board search underway has every reason to say “existing commitments will be honored” and nothing more.

The more useful read will come from the Q3 10-Q, which updates the footnotes behind that $530.5B for the quarter ended in late October. According to the WSJ, that’s the stretch when Nvidia was already pulling back. In late August it paused some of its credit-support deals with cloud providers (guarantees given in exchange for a cut of their revenue) and started requiring executive-team and board sign-off on each one. By October, the WSJ reports, it had begun turning off the tap. If guarantees and cloud buy-back commitments flattened or fell from July’s $108.5B and $36B, the “Bank of Nvidia” was already cutting back even before Huang left.

text:
The Gulf states must finally recognize that US foreign policy, particularly under Donald Trump’s administration, has consistently placed Israel’s security and strategic interests at the center of its Middle East agenda, often at the expense of regional stability and the interests of the Gulf nations themselves.
If the Gulf states genuinely seek peace and stability, they should unequivocally condemn any unlawful American or Israeli military attacks against Iran. Such a position should be followed by a serious reassessment of the continued presence of US  military forces and bases across the Gulf region, including a clear commitment to preventing their territories from being used to launch aggression against neighboring countries.
These would be meaningful confidence-building measures demonstrating genuine goodwill toward Iran and helping restore the trust that has been undermined by decades of regional confrontation.
The Gulf governments cannot simply portray themselves as innocent victims of regional instability while avoiding scrutiny of their military cooperation with Washington. Any allegations of covert financial, logistical, or military support for operations against neighboring states must be investigated transparently.
The region should also remember the disastrous consequences of the 1980s, when several Gulf governments provided substantial financial support to Saddam Hussein during the devastating Iran–Iraq War. That history should serve as a warning against repeating policies that turn neighboring countries into enemies and expose entire populations to decades of suffering.
The conflicts in Syria, Iraq, and Libya offer further lessons about the destructive consequences of foreign intervention, proxy warfare, and support for armed factions. The responsibility of all governments involved deserves serious and impartial examination.
The Gulf states must understand that their long-term security cannot depend indefinitely on foreign military protection, especially when the strategic priorities of those foreign powers may differ from the interests of the region itself.
Real security will not come from hosting more foreign military bases, purchasing billions of dollars in weapons, or participating in endless geopolitical confrontations. It must come from diplomacy, mutual respect, non-aggression, and a genuine regional security framework that includes Iran.
The Gulf belongs to the people of the region. Its future should not be dictated by Washington or Tel Aviv, and its nations must never again allow their territories to become launching pads for wars against their own neighbors.
It is time to replace confrontation with cooperation, dependency with sovereignty, and decades of mistrust with a serious commitment to lasting regional peace.

text:
2027: The Road, The People And President Tinubu's Journey Across Nigeria

By Stanley Nkwocha

Photographs of Nigerian political rallies often capture the scale of the crowd, but they fail to reveal the individual sacrifices and motivations behind it. Whether it is an elderly citizen enduring the midday sun, a young woman travelling kilometres to attend a rally, or a trader leaving behind daily income to see a convoy, every attendee participates for a distinct reason. Rather than representing a single unified voice, these gatherings reflect a complex intersection of personal hardship, hope and civic expectation.

Buoyed by a triumphant reception and the resounding endorsement of party faithful in Kaduna, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu @officialABAT continues to carry the banner of Renewed Hope to every corner of the country. As the race for 2027 unfolds, his message for a second four-year term remains resolute: guiding Nigeria From Reforms to Prosperity.

From the bustling streets of Kaduna to the shores of Calabar, and across Lafia, Ado-Ekiti, Uyo, Port Harcourt, Abakaliki, Dutse, Akure, Benin City and Jos, the message has echoed across the nation. Flanked by Vice President Kashim Shettima @officialSKSM, APC governors, party stalwarts, chieftains and legions of dedicated supporters, the President @NGRPresident has carried the campaign directly to the Nigerian people. This opening leg stands as a triumphant, seamless tour de force, uniting regions and energising the grassroots in a powerful, hitch-free start to the journey ahead.

The cheers have been loud. The receptions have been colourful. Yet beneath the spectacle lies something more consequential. It is a conversation about the sacrifices Nigerians have made, the promises of President Tinubu and the kind of country those sacrifices are expected to produce.

Making his economic agenda the centrepiece of the campaign, President Tinubu is counting on his record to win over voters. As his deputy and political partner, Vice President Shettima has taken that message to communities nationwide, spotlighting the administration's achievements and the unfinished business it intends to complete.

The journey started in Kaduna, where the Nigerian leader formally launched the APC presidential campaign. The choice of venue carried deep political weight. As a historic nerve centre for northern political organisation, national debate and coalition-building, Kaduna set a deliberate stage for the road ahead.

Framing the campaign as the next chapter of a mission launched in 2023, the President confronted the hard realities of his economic reforms head-on. He pledged to turn those difficult choices into lasting progress by driving infrastructure growth, boosting agricultural output, attracting investment and creating jobs. His core message was clear: the sacrifices Nigerians have endured over the past three years must now yield real opportunities and a better standard of living for every citizen.

Invoking a history of political alliances, Vice President Shettima urged the North to remember President Tinubu's decades of support for northern leaders—from Atiku and Ribadu to the late President Buhari.

In public life, people never forget who stood beside them when the future was uncertain. In a political landscape where alliances shift overnight, those shared memories become the bedrock of trust. Speaking in Kaduna, Vice President Shettima made it clear that loyalty, reciprocity and shared history still carry weight in Nigeria's democracy. His message also signalled a clear campaign strategy: rallying the deep personal bonds and foundational alliances that first built the APC.

The campaign subsequently moved to Calabar, Cross River State, where the discussion acquired a different character. At the U.J. Esuene Stadium, Senator Shettima spoke about the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway and the proposed Bakassi Deep Seaport, linking these projects to the future of commerce, investment and employment in the state.

His argument was straightforward. Economic reforms must eventually create opportunities that people can recognise. For a fisherman in Bakassi, development may mean access to better markets. For a young graduate in Calabar, it could mean a job connected to maritime trade, logistics or tourism. For a small business owner, it could mean dependable infrastructure and a more predictable business environment.

In Calabar, VP Shettima also presented President Tinubu's economic restructuring as the groundwork for greater prosperity. That commitment found practical expression on Friday, November 13, when the Vice President, representing President Tinubu, performed the groundbreaking ceremony for the $3.5 billion Bakassi Deep Seaport.

For a project that had remained on the drawing board for decades, the ceremony marked a significant milestone. The administration has presented the seaport as part of its wider ambition to expand maritime trade, attract investment, create jobs and open new economic opportunities for Cross River State and the country.

As the campaign rolled into Lafia, Nasarawa State, attention turned squarely to national integration and infrastructure. Senator Shettima spotlighted the Akwanga–Jos–Bauchi–Gombe–Biu–Maiduguri Superhighway as a vital economic lifeline bridging the North-Central and North-East.

Economists often wrap the value of infrastructure in complex jargon, yet the truth about roads is simple: a good road expands what is possible for people. It decides whether a farmer reaches the market before the harvest spoils, dictates what a trader pays to move goods and determines whether a patient arrives at the hospital in time.

This was the larger meaning of President Tinubu's infrastructure agenda in Nasarawa. The Vice President presented roads as instruments of economic opportunity, connecting communities that have long suffered the consequences of poor access.

The Vice President also visited the Emir of Lafia, where the conversation touched on loyalty, service and the responsibility of political leaders to maintain relationships beyond election seasons.

Then came Ekiti on November 5. If Kaduna emphasised political memory and Nasarawa the economics of infrastructure, Ado-Ekiti brought the language of accountability to the foreground.

"We know the sacrifices you have made, and we are beginning to reap the benefits of those difficult decisions," VP Shettima told the gathering.

He followed that acknowledgment with a review of federal interventions in healthcare, electricity, roads and education. The conversion of the former State Specialist Hospital in Ikole-Ekiti into a Federal Medical Centre, electricity projects in Ilupeju and Ijesa-Isu, road reconstruction and access to student loans through @NELFUND formed part of his account of the administration's work.

But perhaps the most revealing part of the Ekiti rally was the recognition that government must account for what it has done and what remains unfinished. "We have begun to fulfil those commitments, and we have returned to account for the work already done and the tasks that remain," the Vice President said.

That distinction matters because citizens do not experience governance as a collection of press releases. They experience it through the availability of electricity, the condition of roads, the cost of education and the reliability of public services.

Ekiti also offered a picture of shifting political relationships. Former governorship candidates of the PDP, SDP and APM publicly declared support for President Tinubu, while Governor Biodun Oyebanji @biodunaoyebanji pledged to deliver no less than 90 per cent of registered voters.

On Friday, November 6, attention turned to Uyo, Akwa Ibom State, where President Tinubu was joined by Vice President Shettima, governors, party chieftains and other dignitaries for another round of political engagements and the commissioning of projects undertaken by Governor Umo Eno's administration @_PastorUmoEno.

The visit brought federal-state cooperation into sharper focus. The new international terminal at Victor Attah International Airport, the aviation facilities, road projects and other investments represented the state government's effort to expand infrastructure and economic opportunities.

Governor Eno's engagement with the President also illustrated how relationships between Abuja and the states can influence development priorities. For ordinary Nigerians, the constitutional division between federal and state responsibilities matters less than the actual delivery of services. What they want is a road that works, a hospital that functions and public institutions that respond to their needs.

In Port Harcourt, Rivers State, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu took centre stage at the Adokiye Amiesimaka Stadium, where he addressed a massive gathering of supporters alongside Vice President Kashim Shettima and other political leaders. The President thanked the people of Rivers for their support and commended Governor Siminalayi Fubara and the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, for embracing reconciliation after the state's political crisis. His message was that peace and political stability remain essential to development.

President Tinubu also spoke about the economic reforms of his administration, assuring Nigerians that the difficult decisions taken since 2023 were laying the foundation for greater prosperity. He highlighted efforts to clear outstanding pensions and gratuities and reaffirmed his commitment to education, healthcare, youth development and citizens' welfare.

The campaign subsequently reached Abakaliki, Ebonyi State, where President Tinubu's message centred on the opportunities that better infrastructure and economic integration could create for the South-East.

Ebonyi's agricultural strength and growing commercial activities give particular meaning to investments in transport and access to markets. For farmers and traders, the value of development is often measured by how easily their goods can reach buyers and how much of their earnings they can retain.

In Dutse, Jigawa State, VP Shettima accompanied President Tinubu as the campaign turned to agricultural production, vocational training, infrastructure and the future of employment. The President inaugurated projects and presented the APC manifesto, From Reforms to Prosperity, setting out the administration's priorities for the next phase of its economic programme.

The engagements highlighted agricultural mechanisation, skills acquisition, water supply and transport infrastructure. The President's message was that Nigeria must expand its productive capacity and equip more young people to earn a living through enterprise and skilled work.

Akure, Ondo State, brought the discussion back to the relationship between federal economic reforms and development at the state level.

Representing President Tinubu, VP Shettima highlighted increased Federation Account receipts, rural road interventions, the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway, Port Ondo, electricity infrastructure and healthcare improvements.

The Vice President explained that the administration's reforms were intended to give states greater financial capacity to undertake projects and improve public services. He also acknowledged that several commitments remained unfinished.

In Benin City, Edo State, President Tinubu, through his deputy, Vice President Kashim Shettima, placed particular emphasis on his administration's infrastructure and industrial development agenda.

Representing the President, VP Shettima spoke about the rehabilitation of major roads, the dualisation of the Ekpoma–Auchi–Okpella corridor, industrial energy supply through the Obiafu–Obrikom–Oben gas pipeline and federal support for healthcare institutions.

The Vice President also reaffirmed the administration's commitment to the return of the historic Benin Bronzes, recognising the importance of cultural heritage to the identity and dignity of the Benin Kingdom.

"We ask that our stewardship be judged by the lives our decisions have touched and the work we are determined to complete," he told the gathering.

Then came Jos, Plateau State, on November 14, where VP Shettima joined President Tinubu for another major campaign gathering in the Home of Peace and Tourism.

Plateau's agricultural potential, security concerns and road infrastructure gave the visit particular significance. The Akwanga–Jos highway and other federal road interventions formed part of the administration's development agenda for the state.

For Plateau, however, the question of peace remains inseparable from prosperity. Farmers must be able to cultivate their land without fear. Traders need safe roads, and communities need the confidence to rebuild relationships damaged by years of insecurity.

President Tinubu's commitments to infrastructure and economic development speak to these concerns, alongside his administration's responsibility to protect lives and restore lasting peace.

Across these states, President Tinubu's economic agenda has found expression in the different needs of the people. The concerns of ordinary Nigerians are familiar: a father worries about the cost of feeding his family, a mother works long hours to keep her business alive, and a young graduate hopes that years of education will eventually lead to meaningful employment. The President's economic agenda seeks to address these concerns through infrastructure investment, agricultural development, industrial expansion and improved public services.

For Vice President Shettima, travelling across the country has meant explaining that agenda in the language of the communities he meets. He has spoken about the sacrifices Nigerians have made, the progress the administration has reported and the work President Tinubu has committed to completing. His message has remained consistent: the government recognises the difficulties facing ordinary Nigerians and is pursuing reforms intended to improve their lives.

There is also something deeply instructive about the relationship between the President and his deputy on this journey. While President Tinubu leads the campaign and sets out the direction of his administration, Senator Shettima has taken that message to different parts of the country, engaging traditional rulers, political leaders, traders, farmers, young people and ordinary citizens.

The campaign has offered memorable scenes. Stadiums filled with supporters, traditional rulers receiving the presidential delegation, young people waving flags and elderly citizens waiting patiently to see their leaders. But some of the most important moments have come when the speeches turned to matters that affect daily life: the condition of roads, the cost of living, the security of communities and the opportunities available to young Nigerians.

These are the practical concerns around which President Tinubu has framed his development programme. The administration's position is that the reforms undertaken since 2023 have created the basis for stronger public finances, increased investment and a more productive economy. Its continuing responsibility is to translate those changes into improvements that reach households and communities across Nigeria.

As the campaign continues towards the 2027 general elections, President Tinubu and Vice President Shettima will have further opportunities to explain their record, listen to Nigerians and set out their priorities for the years ahead.

For the people who have lined the roads, filled the stadiums and welcomed the campaign across the country, the meaning of development remains wonderfully simple. It is the farmer who gets his produce to market without losing half of it on a bad road. It is the student who can remain in school because an education loan has lifted a burden from the family. It is the trader whose business grows because electricity and transport have become more dependable.

They are the lives behind the statistics and the faces behind the crowds. Above all, their hopes give government its purpose. And that, ultimately, is what President Tinubu's journey across Nigeria is about. It is about the work of turning a national economic programme into opportunities that Nigerians can recognise in their own lives.

- Nkwocha is Senior Special Assistant to the President on Media & Communications (Office of the Vice President) and Chairman of the Media Intelligence Subcommittee of the Strategic Communications Committee of the APC Presidential Campaign Council. He wrote from Abuja.

🚨 From the archives: Mélanie Joly’s “clean slate” for the corrupt — and the pattern that never changed.
In October 2013, while running for mayor of Montreal under True Change for Montreal (Vrai Changement), candidate Mélanie Joly promised an “amnesty” to companies already found guilty of collusion and corruption in awarding public contracts — provided they agreed to compensate Montrealers, change their governance, and “start doing business in a clean way.”
Her words: “It’s time for Montreal to get the money back from engineering firms, and the same time make sure that we can start on a clean slate.”
Other candidates called it what it was: an amnesty. She framed it as pragmatic recovery + jobs. Critics saw it as letting the colluders back in the game after a payment.
She left municipal politics, jumped to the federal Liberals, and is now Industry Minister under Carney.
Fast-forward to the public record:
•  On the SDTC “green slush fund”: roughly $34 million went to ineligible projects. Joly’s response (tabled in Parliament): recovering it was “not in the public interest” and would not constitute “sound stewardship of public funds.” Recipients supposedly acted “in good faith.” The Public Accounts Committee had expressed extreme concern over the disregard of taxpayer money. Liberals blocked further recovery motions. No clawback.
•  On Stellantis Brampton: Ottawa committed up to $529 million (with Ontario adding more) to keep production and jobs. Roughly $222 million had already been paid out. The plant was idled, the Jeep Compass moved to Illinois, 2,000+ workers sidelined. Stellantis sold the facility to Roshel. Lobbying records show senior aides in Joly’s office (including then-chief of staff and policy director) and PMO met with Roshel in August, September, and October — before the public announcement. Her office says she personally never met Roshel and was only mediating with the union; the government never supported the sale. After the news broke: default notice, “on the hook for hundreds of millions,” tough talk. Stellantis offers $24 million back. Talk of another “aggressive package” of public money. No one fired. Contracts remain heavily redacted with escape clauses.
The 2013 proposal was explicit: companies found guilty of collusion and corruption get a path back if they pay something and promise to be better. The ministerial record shows the same instinct — recovery is optional when it is inconvenient, “public interest” and “sound stewardship” are invoked to leave the money with the recipients, and public outrage is met with press conferences rather than consequences.
Montrealers in 2013 were told the colluders would compensate them and clean up. Canadians in 2026 are told $34 million is not worth pursuing and that Stellantis is “on the hook” for hundreds of millions while the actual offer is a fraction of what was paid out.
Same instinct. Different file. The receipts are public.
#cdnpoli

BIG: Jensen Huang resigned as NVIDIA President, CEO, and board member, effective immediately, board accepted 11 Nov. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO, Harvey C. Jones is first-ever board chair.
Elon Musk publicly signed a petition for Jensen Huang's reinstatement, according to what I'm hearing.
NVIDIA board reportedly approached Rene Haas, CEO of Arm, as a possible successor, according to what I'm hearing.

BIG: ChatGPT Wallet launched 13 Nov. Agents can buy things for you, with your approval, using Visa, Mastercard, and Amex. Early access only for eligible US ChatGPT Pro users.

BIG: Anthropic IPO 6x oversubscribed. An IPO is when a company sells its shares to the public for the first time, so anyone can buy a part of the company. 825 million shares, $70-78 per share, ticker ANT on Nasdaq. A ticker is the short code used to trade a company on the stock market. Pricing 18 Nov, trading 19 Nov. Total value ~$64bn, ~$1.4tn valuation.

Gemini 4 Hydrogen, 12 Nov, $8.25 per 1M tokens.
Claude Fable 5.2, 9 Nov, $40 per 1M tokens.
DeepSeek API, 13 Nov. Search, document reading, URL reading, OCR, voice to text, text to voice. OCR is a tool that reads text from a photo or a document.

United Airlines banned AI agents from booking, 11 Nov.
Anthropic Claude Meetings in beta, for paid Team and Enterprise. Beta means a test version, not the final version yet.

2. AI Agents
United Airlines banned AI agents from booking, 11 Nov.
Notion breach, Fireworks AI, fewer than 1% of workspaces.
Baidu Famou 3.0, self-evolving super agent. A super agent is an AI that can learn and improve on its own while doing work, and can do many different tasks by itself, not just one task.
Alibaba Cloud AgentCore supports DeepSeek Harness.
See AI section for ChatGPT Wallet.

3. AGI
GPT-6 Astra got 74.8% on robot manipulation, better than 51.0% for specialist models.
Claude Fable 5.2 topped RoboColiseum with 18.30 points. RoboColiseum is a leaderboard, a ranking list, that tests robots on how well they move and handle things.
OpenAI split robotics team into core research and applied / hardware.
Most probably, 2027 will be the AGI race year.

4. Fab / Semiconductor
IBM Nighthawk r3, 520 qubits. IBM Nighthawk r3 is IBM's newest quantum computer chip, with 520 qubits, the most powerful one IBM has made so far. It is built to solve very hard problems that normal computers cannot solve fast.
Foxconn targets automotive chiplets with 5μm fan-out RDL packaging, 15 Nov. A chiplet is a small chip, many small chips are joined together to make one big powerful chip. Fan-out RDL is a way to pack these small chips tightly together in a car chip, so it runs faster and uses less power. 5μm is the size, very tiny, smaller than a hair.
NVIDIA 260,000 GPU commitment to South Korea remains intact, South Korea said.

5. GPU / CPU
NVIDIA earnings Tue 17 Nov, after Jensen resignation.
Shares fell ~10-14% after resignation.
llama.cpp 1.0 released 13 Nov. Stable API, FP8, better local LLM running. FP8 is a faster way for AI to do maths, so it runs faster on a normal computer.

6. Quantum
IBM Nighthawk r3, 520 qubits. See Fab section for full details.
QuiX Quantum leads mission to develop 100+ qubit photonic quantum computer. Photonic means it uses light, not electricity, to compute.

7. Smartphones
Vivo X500 India launch 26 Nov, MRPs leaked up to ₹2,14,999, according to what I'm hearing. MRP is the maximum retail price, the highest price a shop can sell it for.
OnePlus N6 Lite 4G launched India 14 Nov, 7,000mAh. mAh is battery size, bigger number means longer battery life.
Samsung Tab A11+ +₹3,000. OnePlus Pad 4 ₹60,000 to ₹98,000.
Redmi hikes from Mon 16 Nov, A7 +₹2,000, Note 17 Pro 5G +₹4,000. Buy before Monday if you were planning to.
Reno 17 launch Mon 16 Nov.

text:
A group of 10 companies, including OpenAI, TikTok, Adobe, the BBC, and the dating app Bumble, have signed up to a new set of guidelines on how to build, create, and share AI-generated content responsibly. 

The recommendations call for both the builders of the technology, such as OpenAI, and creators and distributors of digitally created synthetic media, such as the BBC and TikTok, to be more transparent about what the technology can and cannot do, and disclose when people might be interacting with this type of content. 

The voluntary recommendations were put together by the Partnership on AI (PAI), an AI research nonprofit, in consultation with over 50 organizations. PAI’s partners include big tech companies as well as academic, civil society, and media organizations. The first 10 companies to commit to the guidance are Adobe, BBC, CBC/Radio-Canada, Bumble, OpenAI, TikTok, Witness, and synthetic-media startups Synthesia, D-ID, and Respeecher. 

“We want to ensure that synthetic media is not used to harm, disempower, or disenfranchise but rather to support creativity, knowledge sharing, and commentary,” says Claire Leibowicz, PAI’s head of AI and media integrity. 

One of the most important elements of the guidelines is a pact by the companies to include and research ways to tell users when they’re interacting with something that’s been generated by AI. This might include watermarks or disclaimers, or traceable elements in an AI model’s training data or metadata. 

Regulation attempting to rein in potential harms relating to generative AI is still lagging behind. The European Union, for example, is trying to include generative AI in its upcoming AI law, the AI Act, which could include elements such as disclosing when people are interacting with deepfakes and obligating companies to meet certain transparency requirements. 

While generative AI is a Wild West right now, says Henry Ajder, an expert on generative AI who contributed to the guidelines, he hopes they will offer companies key things they need to look out for as they incorporate the technology into their businesses.

Raising awareness and starting a conversation around responsible ways to think about synthetic media is important, says Hany Farid, a professor at the University of California, Berkeley, who researches synthetic media and deepfakes. 

But “voluntary guidelines and principles rarely work,” he adds. 

While companies such as OpenAI can try to put guardrails on technologies they create, like ChatGPT and DALL-E, other players that are not part of the pact—such as https://t.co/G133p3BVPF, the startup that created the open source image-generating AI model Stable Diffusion—can let people generate inappropriate images and deepfakes.  

“If we really want to address these issues, we’ve got to get serious,” says Farid. For example, he wants cloud service providers and app stores such as those operated by Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and Apple, which are all part of the PAI, to ban services that allow people to use deepfake technology with the intent to create nonconsensual sexual imagery. Watermarks on all AI-generated content should also be mandated, not voluntary, he says. 

Another important thing missing is how the AI systems themselves could be made more responsible, says Ilke Demir, a senior research scientist at Intel who leads the company’s work on the responsible development of generative AI. This could include more details on how the AI model was trained, what data went into it, and whether generative AI models have any biases. 

The guidelines have no mention of ensuring that there’s no toxic content in the data set of generative AI models. “It’s one of the most significant ways harm is caused by these systems,” says Daniel Leufer, a senior policy analyst at the digital rights group Access Now. 

The guidelines include a list of harms that these companies want to prevent, such as fraud, harassment, and disinformation. But a generative AI model that always creates white people is also doing harm, and that is not currently listed, adds Demir.

Farid raises a more fundamental issue. Since the companies acknowledge that the technology could lead to some serious harms and offer ways to mitigate them, “why aren’t they asking the question ‘Should we do this in the first place?’”

text:
🕹️ The History of Video Games in 300 Moments

🔬 THE LAB ERA (1947–1971)

𝟏. 1947: Goldsmith and Mann patent a "cathode-ray tube amusement device", often called the first electronic game.

𝟐. 1950: Bertie the Brain, a 4 m tall tic-tac-toe computer, wows visitors in Toronto 🇨🇦.

𝟑. 1951: The Nimrod computer plays the game Nim at the Festival of Britain 🇬🇧.

𝟒. 1952: A.S. Douglas writes OXO, a noughts-and-crosses game, on Cambridge's EDSAC computer.

𝟓. 1958: William Higinbotham shows Tennis for Two on an oscilloscope in New York 🇺🇸.

𝟔. 1962: Steve Russell and friends at MIT create Spacewar! on a PDP-1 computer.

𝟕. 1962: Spacewar! spreads from lab to lab and inspires a generation of programmers.

𝟖. 1966: Engineer Ralph Baer writes down his idea of playing games on a home TV.

𝟗. 1968: Baer's "Brown Box" prototype, the ancestor of every home console, is up and running.

𝟏𝟎. 1971: Galaxy Game, a coin-operated Spacewar!, is installed at Stanford University.

𝟏𝟏. 1971: Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney release Computer Space, the first commercial arcade video game.

𝟏𝟐. 1971: Computer Space reportedly sells only about 1,500 units: too complex for bar customers.

𝟏𝟑. 1971: Three student teachers in Minnesota write the first version of The Oregon Trail.

🕹️ PONG & THE FIRST CONSOLES (1972–1977)

𝟏𝟒. 1972: Baer's design becomes the Magnavox Odyssey, the first home video game console.

𝟏𝟓. 1972: The Odyssey has no sound and uses plastic overlays on the TV screen.

𝟏𝟔. 1972: Bushnell and Dabney found Atari in California.

𝟏𝟕. 1972: Allan Alcorn builds Pong, originally as a training exercise.

𝟏𝟖. 1972: Legend says the first Pong test machine broke because its coin box overflowed.

𝟏𝟗. 1973: Maze War, one of the first first-person shooters, appears at NASA.

𝟐𝟎. 1974: Atari's Gran Trak 10 is among the first arcade racing games.

𝟐𝟏. 1975: Home Pong is sold through the US retailer Sears and becomes a Christmas hit.

𝟐𝟐. 1975: Gun Fight is one of the first arcade games to use a microprocessor.

𝟐𝟑. 1976: Atari settles Magnavox's lawsuit over Pong's similarity to the Odyssey's table tennis.

𝟐𝟒. 1976: The Fairchild Channel F is the first console with swappable ROM cartridges.

𝟐𝟓. 1976: Its cartridge team is led by Jerry Lawson, a pioneering Black engineer.

𝟐𝟔. 1976: Will Crowther's Colossal Cave Adventure starts the adventure genre.

𝟐𝟕. 1976: The arcade game Death Race sparks the first big public outcry over video game violence.

𝟐𝟖. 1976: Warner Communications buys Atari for about $28 million.

𝟐𝟗. 1976: Atari releases Breakout; Steve Wozniak and Steve Jobs worked on its prototype.

𝟑𝟎. 1977: The Atari VCS, later called the 2600, launches with joysticks and cartridges.

𝟑𝟏. 1977: The 2600 goes on to sell about 30 million units.

𝟑𝟐. 1977: Nintendo enters home video games in Japan 🇯🇵 with the Color TV-Game 6.

👾 THE GOLDEN AGE OF ARCADES (1978–1982)

𝟑𝟑. 1978: Tomohiro Nishikado creates Space Invaders for Taito.

𝟑𝟒. 1978: Space Invaders is said to have caused a 100-yen coin shortage in Japan, a disputed claim.

𝟑𝟓. 1978: Roy Trubshaw and Richard Bartle create MUD1 in England 🇬🇧, the first multi-user dungeon.

𝟑𝟔. 1979: Asteroids becomes Atari's best-selling arcade machine.

𝟑𝟕. 1979: Four former Atari programmers found Activision, the first third-party console game developer.

𝟑𝟖. 1979: Namco's Galaxian brings full-colour graphics to the arcade.

𝟑𝟗. 1979: Milton Bradley's Microvision is the first handheld with interchangeable cartridges.

𝟒𝟎. 1980: Toru Iwatani's Pac-Man arrives in arcades.

𝟒𝟏. 1980: Iwatani said Pac-Man's shape was inspired by a pizza with a slice missing.

𝟒𝟐. 1980: In Japan the game was called Puck Man; the name was changed abroad.

𝟒𝟑. 1980: Blinky, Pinky, Inky and Clyde each chase Pac-Man in a different way.

𝟒𝟒. 1980: The US Army reportedly commissions a training version of Battlezone.

𝟒𝟓. 1980: Space Invaders on the Atari 2600 is the first licensed arcade port.

𝟒𝟔. 1980: Warren Robinett hides his name in Atari's Adventure, one of the first known Easter eggs.

𝟒𝟕. 1980: Rogue's random dungeons give the "roguelike" genre its name.

𝟒𝟖. 1980: Infocom releases Zork I, a landmark of text adventures.

𝟒𝟗. 1980: Gunpei Yokoi's Game & Watch handhelds launch at Nintendo.

𝟓𝟎. 1980: Missile Command puts players in charge of defending cities from nuclear attack.

𝟓𝟏. 1981: Shigeru Miyamoto's Donkey Kong introduces Jumpman, soon renamed Mario.

𝟓𝟐. 1981: Mario was reportedly named after Mario Segale, Nintendo of America's landlord.

𝟓𝟑. 1981: Williams' Defender scrolls across a world bigger than the screen.

𝟓𝟒. 1981: Konami's Frogger and Namco's Galaga become arcade staples.

𝟓𝟓. 1981: Ultima and Wizardry lay the foundations of computer role-playing games.

𝟓𝟔. 1982: Ms. Pac-Man, born as an unofficial upgrade kit, becomes a US arcade smash.

𝟓𝟕. 1982: The Commodore 64 launches; estimates of its sales run from 12 to 17 million.

𝟓𝟖. 1982: The ZX Spectrum kicks off the bedroom-coding scene in the UK 🇬🇧.

𝟓𝟗. 1982: Electronic Arts is founded by Trip Hawkins.

𝟔𝟎. 1982: David Crane's Pitfall! for Activision is one of the first side-scrolling platform games.

𝟔𝟏. 1982: ColecoVision launches with Donkey Kong as its pack-in game.

𝟔𝟐. 1982: Namco's Pole Position becomes the top-earning arcade game in North America in 1983.

𝟔𝟑. 1982: Atari's rushed Pac-Man port for the 2600 sells millions but disappoints players.

𝟔𝟒. 1982: Howard Scott Warshaw makes the E.T. game in about five weeks.

💥 THE CRASH & THE COMEBACK (1983–1988)

𝟔𝟓. 1983: Dragon's Lair, animated by Don Bluth on laserdisc, costs 50 cents a play.

𝟔𝟔. 1983: The North American video game market crashes; revenues fall by about 97% by 1985.

𝟔𝟕. 1983: Atari buries unsold cartridges in a landfill in Alamogordo, New Mexico 🇺🇸.

𝟔𝟖. 1983: Nintendo releases the Famicom in Japan 🇯🇵 on 15 July.

𝟔𝟗. 1983: Sega's first home console, the SG-1000, launches the very same day.

𝟕𝟎. 1983: Mario Bros. introduces his brother Luigi.

𝟕𝟏. 1983: Microsoft and ASCII announce the MSX home computer standard.

𝟕𝟐. 1984: Alexey Pajitnov creates Tetris at a Soviet computing centre in Moscow.

𝟕𝟑. 1984: The name Tetris combines "tetra" (four) and tennis, Pajitnov's favourite sport.

𝟕𝟒. 1984: David Braben and Ian Bell's Elite squeezes a 3D space universe into a BBC Micro.

𝟕𝟓. 1984: Roberta Williams' King's Quest brings animated graphics to adventure games.

𝟕𝟔. 1985: The Nintendo Entertainment System test-launches in New York 🇺🇸.

𝟕𝟕. 1985: Nintendo bundles R.O.B. the robot so shops will treat the NES as a toy.

𝟕𝟖. 1985: Nintendo's Seal of Quality limits shovelware, which had helped cause the crash.

𝟕𝟗. 1985: Super Mario Bros. arrives and goes on to sell over 40 million copies.

𝟖𝟎. 1985: Atari Games' Gauntlet lets four players fight side by side in the arcade.

𝟖𝟏. 1985: The Commodore Amiga launches with advanced graphics and sound.

𝟖𝟐. 1986: The Legend of Zelda debuts, inspired by Miyamoto's childhood explorations around Kyoto.

𝟖𝟑. 1986: Yuji Horii's Dragon Quest, with art by Akira Toriyama, makes RPGs a craze in Japan.

𝟖𝟒. 1986: Metroid surprises players by revealing hero Samus Aran as a woman.

𝟖𝟓. 1986: Yu Suzuki's Out Run lets players choose the music on the car radio.

𝟖𝟔. 1987: Square releases Final Fantasy; legend says it was named as a possible last game.

𝟖𝟕. 1987: Hideo Kojima's Metal Gear launches stealth action on the MSX2.

𝟖𝟖. 1987: Capcom releases Street Fighter and Mega Man.

𝟖𝟗. 1987: NEC's PC Engine, known as the TurboGrafx-16 in the West, launches in Japan.

𝟗𝟎. 1987: Maniac Mansion debuts the SCUMM engine behind many LucasArts adventures.

𝟗𝟏. 1988: Sega launches the Mega Drive in Japan.

𝟗𝟐. 1988: Super Mario Bros. 3 is released in Japan and later sells over 17 million copies.

𝟗𝟑. 1988: Nintendo Power magazine launches in the US.

𝟗𝟒. 1988: John Madden Football (1988) starts a sports series that still runs every year.

🦔 THE 16-BIT WARS (1989–1995)

𝟗𝟓. 1989: Gunpei Yokoi's Game Boy launches in Japan.

𝟗𝟔. 1989: Tetris is bundled with the Game Boy in North America and becomes a global obsession.

𝟗𝟕. 1989: The Game Boy line, including the Color, sells about 119 million units.

𝟗𝟖. 1989: The Atari Lynx is the first handheld with a colour LCD.

𝟗𝟗. 1989: Will Wright's SimCity creates a game you cannot really win.

𝟏𝟎𝟎. 1989: Jordan Mechner animates Prince of Persia by filming his brother running and jumping.

𝟏𝟎𝟏. 1989: The Sega Genesis arrives in North America.

𝟏𝟎𝟐. 1990: Nintendo releases the Super Famicom in Japan.

𝟏𝟎𝟑. 1990: Launch title Super Mario World introduces Yoshi.

𝟏𝟎𝟒. 1990: id Software's Commander Keen shows smooth scrolling on PCs.

𝟏𝟎𝟓. 1990: SNK launches the Neo Geo, with arcade-quality games at home.

𝟏𝟎𝟔. 1991: Sonic the Hedgehog gives Sega a fast, cool mascot to rival Mario.

𝟏𝟎𝟕. 1991: Sega's slogan "Genesis does what Nintendon't" fuels the console war.

𝟏𝟎𝟖. 1991: Street Fighter II sets off a worldwide fighting game boom.

𝟏𝟎𝟗. 1991: Its combos reportedly began as a happy programming accident.

𝟏𝟏𝟎. 1991: Sid Meier's Civilization launches the "one more turn" genre.

𝟏𝟏𝟏. 1991: Nintendo's SNES arrives in North America.

𝟏𝟏𝟐. 1991: The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past arrives on the Super Famicom.

𝟏𝟏𝟑. 1991: DMA Design in Scotland 🇬🇧 releases Lemmings.

𝟏𝟏𝟒. 1992: Mortal Kombat's digitised actors and gory "fatalities" cause outrage.

𝟏𝟏𝟓. 1992: Wolfenstein 3D popularises the first-person shooter.

𝟏𝟏𝟔. 1992: Alone in the Dark lays the groundwork for 3D survival horror.

𝟏𝟏𝟕. 1992: Super Mario Kart popularises the kart racing genre.

𝟏𝟏𝟖. 1992: Westwood's Dune II sets the template for real-time strategy.

𝟏𝟏𝟗. 1992: Sega launches Sonic 2 worldwide on "Sonic 2sday", a Tuesday in November.

𝟏𝟐𝟎. 1993: id Software releases Doom on 10 December.

𝟏𝟐𝟏. 1993: Doom's first episode is free as shareware and spreads everywhere.

𝟏𝟐𝟐. 1993: Doom popularises the word "deathmatch".

𝟏𝟐𝟑. 1993: US Senate hearings on video game violence follow Mortal Kombat and Night Trap.

𝟏𝟐𝟒. 1993: Myst becomes a CD-ROM phenomenon and is long the best-selling PC game.

𝟏𝟐𝟓. 1993: Star Fox uses the Super FX chip to bring 3D polygons to the SNES.

𝟏𝟐𝟔. 1993: The Atari Jaguar is marketed as the first "64-bit" console.

𝟏𝟐𝟕. 1993: Sega's Virtua Fighter is the first 3D fighting game.

𝟏𝟐𝟖. 1994: The ESRB age rating system is founded in North America.

𝟏𝟐𝟗. 1994: Sony launches the PlayStation in Japan 🇯🇵 on 3 December.

𝟏𝟑𝟎. 1994: The PlayStation grew out of a failed CD add-on deal between Sony and Nintendo.

𝟏𝟑𝟏. 1994: Sega launches the Saturn in Japan.

𝟏𝟑𝟐. 1994: Rare's Donkey Kong Country stuns players with pre-rendered 3D graphics.

𝟏𝟑𝟑. 1994: Blizzard releases Warcraft: Orcs & Humans.

𝟏𝟑𝟒. 1994: Super Metroid perfects the exploration style later called "Metroidvania".

𝟏𝟑𝟓. 1995: The first E3 expo is held in Los Angeles.

𝟏𝟑𝟔. 1995: At E3 Sega surprise-launches the Saturn at $399; Sony answers with one word on stage: "$299".

𝟏𝟑𝟕. 1995: Square's "Dream Team" releases Chrono Trigger.

𝟏𝟑𝟖. 1995: Nintendo's Virtual Boy flops and is discontinued within about a year.

𝟏𝟑𝟗. 1995: Microsoft's DirectX helps turn Windows into a gaming platform.

𝟏𝟒𝟎. 1995: Command & Conquer popularises RTS online and over local networks.

💿 THE 3D REVOLUTION (1996–1999)

𝟏𝟒𝟏. 1996: The Nintendo 64 launches in Japan.

𝟏𝟒𝟐. 1996: Super Mario 64 shows how to move in 3D with an analogue stick.

𝟏𝟒𝟔. 1996: Capcom's Resident Evil popularises the term "survival horror".

𝟏𝟒𝟕. 1996: Quake brings true 3D worlds and online multiplayer to PCs.

𝟏𝟒𝟖. 1996: Blizzard releases Diablo along with its free online service, https://t.co/HRjdI4HaQs.

𝟏𝟒𝟗. 1996: Bandai's Tamagotchi virtual pet becomes a global craze.

𝟏𝟓𝟎. 1996: Naughty Dog's Crash Bandicoot becomes an early PlayStation mascot.

𝟏𝟓𝟏. 1997: Final Fantasy VII becomes a worldwide hit and makes JRPGs mainstream in the West.

𝟏𝟓𝟐. 1997: Rare's GoldenEye 007 makes split-screen multiplayer a sleepover ritual.

𝟏𝟓𝟑. 1997: Ultima Online popularises the massively multiplayer online game.

𝟏𝟓𝟒. 1997: In a test, a player kills Lord British, creator Richard Garriott's usually invulnerable character.

𝟏𝟓𝟓. 1997: Nokia's 6110 phone comes with Snake, a mobile game for millions 🇫🇮.

𝟏𝟓𝟔. 1997: DMA Design releases the first Grand Theft Auto.

𝟏𝟓𝟕. 1997: Gran Turismo sets a new bar for realistic racing.

𝟏𝟓𝟖. 1997: Sony's DualShock brings two analogue sticks and rumble to the PlayStation.

𝟏𝟓𝟗. 1997: Microsoft releases Age of Empires.

𝟏𝟔𝟎. 1997: Interplay's Fallout drops players into a post-nuclear wasteland.

𝟏𝟔𝟏. 1998: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time introduces Z-targeting.

𝟏𝟔𝟐. 1998: Valve's Half-Life tells its story without cutscenes.

𝟏𝟔𝟑. 1998: StarCraft is released and becomes a TV sport in South Korea 🇰🇷.

𝟏𝟔𝟒. 1998: Metal Gear Solid brings cinematic stealth to the PlayStation.

𝟏𝟔𝟓. 1998: Sega's Dreamcast launches in Japan with a built-in modem.

𝟏𝟔𝟔. 1998: Nintendo releases the Game Boy Color.

𝟏𝟔𝟕. 1998: Pokémon reaches North America and the anime spreads worldwide.

𝟏𝟔𝟖. 1998: Konami's Dance Dance Revolution puts a dance floor in the arcade.

𝟏𝟔𝟗. 1999: EverQuest hooks so many players it is nicknamed "EverCrack".

𝟏𝟕𝟎. 1999: Counter-Strike starts as a fan-made mod for Half-Life.

𝟏𝟕𝟏. 1999: The Dreamcast launches in North America on 9/9/99.

𝟏𝟕𝟐. 1999: Sega's Shenmue is reportedly among the most expensive games made up to that time.

𝟏𝟕𝟑. 1999: Unreal Tournament and Quake III Arena push online arena shooters.

𝟏𝟕𝟓. 2000: The PS2 becomes the best-selling console ever, at more than 160 million units.

𝟏𝟕𝟔. 2000: Will Wright's The Sims becomes one of PC's biggest hits.

𝟏𝟕𝟕. 2000: Blizzard's Diablo II becomes a huge online action-RPG hit.

𝟏𝟕𝟖. 2000: Deus Ex shows how player choice can shape a story.

𝟏𝟕𝟗. 2001: Microsoft enters the market with the Xbox.

𝟏𝟖𝟎. 2001: Halo: Combat Evolved shows that shooters can work on a gamepad.

𝟏𝟖𝟏. 2001: Nintendo launches the GameCube and the Game Boy Advance.

𝟏𝟖𝟐. 2001: Sega stops making consoles and becomes a third-party publisher.

𝟏𝟖𝟑. 2001: Grand Theft Auto III creates the modern open-world 3D city.

𝟏𝟖𝟒. 2002: Xbox Live brings online multiplayer and voice chat to consoles.

𝟏𝟖𝟖. 2003: Valve launches Steam, now the world's largest PC game store.

𝟏𝟗𝟎. 2003: Nokia's N-Gage tries to combine a phone with a game console.

𝟏𝟗𝟏. 2004: World of Warcraft launches; it later peaks at about 12 million subscribers.

𝟏𝟗𝟐. 2004: The dual-screen, touch-screen Nintendo DS launches.

𝟏𝟗𝟒. 2004: Half-Life 2 puts realistic physics and the Gravity Gun in players' hands.

𝟏𝟗𝟔. 2005: The Xbox 360 launches and popularises Achievements.

𝟏𝟗𝟕. 2005: Guitar Hero turns plastic guitars into a global party craze.

𝟏𝟗𝟖. 2005: Nintendo's Brain Age attracts older non-gamers.

𝟏𝟗𝟗. 2005: Nintendogs puts virtual puppies on the DS.

𝟐𝟎𝟐. 2006: The PlayStation 3 launches at $499 and $599 with a Blu-ray drive.

𝟐𝟎𝟑. 2006: Roblox launches, later becoming a platform for millions of user-made games.

𝟐𝟎𝟒. 2006: Gears of War popularises the cover-based shooter.

𝟐𝟎𝟕. 2007: BioShock's underwater city of Rapture asks big questions about free will.

𝟐𝟎𝟖. 2007: Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare reshapes online shooters.

𝟐𝟐𝟕. 2011: Terraria launches and goes on to sell tens of millions of copies.

text:
At 9 years old, Jensen Huang was cleaning toilets in a boarding school in Kentucky.
Today, he leads NVIDIA, one of the most valuable companies in human history.
But the journey between those two points is far more interesting than the money, the black leather jacket, or the billions of dollars.
Because NVIDIA almost died before the world knew what it was.
And the decisions that saved it were not always popular.
Let's go back to the beginning.
Jensen was born in Taiwan in 1963. When he was about five, his family moved to Thailand.
His parents eventually became concerned about the safety and future of their children. So they made a difficult decision.
They sent Jensen and his older brother to America ahead of them.
Jensen was only nine.
Imagine being that young, leaving your parents behind, travelling to another country, and trying to find your place in a world you barely understand.
But things became even more difficult.
His uncle wanted the boys to receive a good education, so he enrolled them in a boarding school in Kentucky.
There was just one problem.
It wasn't the kind of school he thought it was.
The school was actually a religious reform school for troubled teenagers.
Jensen was one of the youngest students there. He struggled with English, had a strong accent, and was one of the few Asian children.
Some of the older students were violent. His roommate was 17 and had scars from being stabbed.
And what was Jensen's daily responsibility?
Cleaning toilets.
Every single day.
But something interesting happened.
His roommate couldn't read, while Jensen could.
So they made a deal.
Jensen would teach him how to read, and in return, the older boy would teach him how to become stronger.
They became friends.
Think about that for a moment.
A nine-year-old boy, thousands of miles away from his parents, found a way to survive by identifying what someone else needed and offering something in return.
Years later, Jensen and his wife would donate $2 million to that same school to help build a dormitory and classroom building for girls.
He didn't forget where he came from.
When his parents eventually joined him in America, the family settled in Oregon.
Jensen attended Aloha High School, skipped two grades, and graduated at just 16.
He was interested in mathematics, computers, and engineering.
But he also needed money.
At 15, he got a job at Denny's, an American restaurant chain.
He started as a dishwasher.
Then he became a busboy, clearing tables, and eventually a waiter.
He worked overnight shifts while going to school.
Years later, he would say that the job helped him overcome his shyness and taught him how to work under pressure.
Interestingly, those restaurant jobs are still part of his professional story.
But nobody working alongside that teenager could have imagined what he would eventually build.
Jensen went on to study electrical engineering at Oregon State University.
After graduating, he worked as a chip designer at AMD and later joined LSI Logic.
He also attended Stanford at night, eventually earning a master's degree in electrical engineering.
By his late twenties, he had a stable career and a comfortable future.
He could have stayed there.
But he didn't.
In 1993, three engineers walked into a Denny's restaurant in San Jose, California.
Their names were Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem.
They sat in a booth, drank cheap coffee, and discussed an idea.
They wanted to build computer chips that would make video games look better.
That was the original idea behind NVIDIA.
Not artificial intelligence.
Not ChatGPT.
Not the technology powering the world's biggest data centres.
Just better graphics for video games.
They believed computers would eventually need special chips to handle increasingly realistic graphics.
Many people weren't convinced.
But the three founders took the risk.
They raised money, hired engineers, and started building.
Then came their first major mistake.
Their first graphics chip, the NV1, used a different approach from what most of the industry was adopting.
It was an intelligent idea on paper, but the rest of the industry was moving in another direction.
Game developers were building around triangles, while NVIDIA had chosen curved surfaces.
The result?
Their chip struggled to work with the software developers were already using.
Sales were disappointing.
The next product was also built around the same flawed approach.
Money started disappearing.
And the company was running out of time.
At one point, NVIDIA was roughly 30 days away from going out of business.
Let that sink in.
The company that would eventually become a multi-trillion-dollar business was once struggling to survive another month.
Jensen had a difficult decision to make.
He could continue pretending everything was fine, or admit that the technology they had built wasn't going to work.
He chose to admit the mistake.
But there was another problem.
NVIDIA had a contract with Sega, the Japanese video game company.
Jensen knew they couldn't deliver the product as originally promised.
So he travelled to Japan to meet a Sega executive named Shoichiro Irimajiri.
He explained the situation honestly.
He told him that NVIDIA couldn't deliver the chip in the way they had planned.
Then he made an unusual request.
He asked Sega to pay the remaining $5 million anyway.
Not because NVIDIA had delivered everything perfectly, but because the company needed the money to survive.
Sega could have walked away.
Instead, the executive agreed.
That $5 million gave NVIDIA the time it desperately needed.
Think about it.
Sometimes, the difference between a business that survives and one that disappears isn't a perfect business plan.
Sometimes, it's one person willing to trust you when you have very little left to offer.
But the money wasn't enough on its own.
NVIDIA had to change direction.
The company abandoned its original graphics approach and focused on the technology the wider industry was adopting.
It developed the RIVA 128 graphics chip.
The product was a success.
NVIDIA reportedly sold around a million units within its first four months.
The company that had nearly disappeared was back in the game.
In 1999, NVIDIA went public.
That same year, it introduced the GeForce 256 and helped establish the term GPU, short for Graphics Processing Unit.
At the time, these chips were mainly associated with gaming.
But Jensen noticed something other people were overlooking.
Scientists and researchers were beginning to use graphics chips for work that had nothing to do with video games.
And that observation would lead to the biggest decision in NVIDIA's history.
In 2006, NVIDIA introduced CUDA.
To understand why this mattered, imagine two kitchens.
The first has one extremely talented chef who can prepare almost any meal, but can only prepare one dish at a time.
The second has thousands of cooks, each handling a small part of the work at the same time.
The first kitchen is similar to a CPU.
The second is similar to a GPU.
A GPU can perform thousands of smaller calculations at once.
This makes it incredibly useful for certain types of scientific research, simulations, and artificial intelligence.
But there was a problem.
Using graphics chips for these other tasks was difficult.
So NVIDIA created CUDA, a system that allowed developers to write software that could use the power of its GPUs for much more than graphics.
Here is where Jensen made another unpopular decision.
He didn't reserve this technology for expensive, specialised chips.
He invested in making it available across NVIDIA's product range, including gaming graphics cards.
It cost money.
Investors questioned the decision.
For years, the investment affected profits, and many people wondered why a company known for gaming was spending so much on software that most of its customers barely used.
Jensen continued anyway.
NVIDIA made the tools available, supported universities, and helped train developers to use them.
He was building something that might not pay off immediately.
And that is what makes this decision so important.
He wasn't just selling computer chips anymore.
He was building an entire ecosystem around them.
Years later, researchers at the University of Toronto used two NVIDIA gaming graphics cards to train a system called AlexNet.
In 2012, that system achieved a remarkable result in a major image-recognition competition.
It showed the research world just how powerful GPUs could be for deep learning.
Suddenly, the same type of chips people bought to play video games could help computers learn to recognise images.
NVIDIA had spent years preparing for a market that was only beginning to emerge.
And it wasn't finished.
In 2016, Jensen personally delivered NVIDIA's first DGX-1 supercomputer to a young research organisation called OpenAI.
At the time, very few people understood just how important artificial intelligence would become.
Then came November 2022.
OpenAI released ChatGPT.
Millions of people started interacting with AI in a completely new way.
Businesses wanted their own AI systems.
Researchers wanted more computing power.
Technology companies began building enormous data centres.
And almost everyone needed the same thing:
NVIDIA's chips.
The H100 became one of the most sought-after pieces of technology in the world.
The company that started by making graphics cards for video games had become central to the artificial intelligence revolution.
Its market value climbed from $1 trillion in 2023 to $2 trillion, then $3 trillion, and eventually reached $5 trillion in 2025.
Jensen became a global celebrity.
The black leather jacket became his signature.
World leaders wanted meetings with him. People lined up for pictures and autographs.
But there is something important about this story that people often overlook.
NVIDIA didn't become what it is today because of one lucky moment.
It was built through decades of decisions.
Some worked.
Some failed.
The company struggled with product mistakes, competition, financial crises, failed market entries, and missed opportunities.
It also made major investments that looked questionable at the time.
One of the most important was CUDA.
Without years of investment in that software ecosystem, NVIDIA's position in the AI industry could look very different today.
And that brings us to another lesson.
Sometimes, the biggest opportunities are hidden inside things that other people don't take seriously.
But success doesn't mean the journey is always upward.
Even today, NVIDIA faces serious questions.
There are concerns about the enormous spending on artificial intelligence, whether the current AI boom can justify its cost, competition from other chipmakers, and restrictions on selling advanced chips to China.
There are also questions about the way money moves between NVIDIA and some of the companies buying its technology.
