Today, he leads NVIDIA, one of the most valuable companies in human history.
But the journey between those two points is far more interesting than the money, the black leather jacket, or the billions of dollars.
Because NVIDIA almost died before the world knew what it was.
And the decisions that saved it were not always popular.
Let's go back to the beginning.
Jensen was born in Taiwan in 1963. When he was about five, his family moved to Thailand.
His parents eventually became concerned about the safety and future of their children. So they made a difficult decision.
They sent Jensen and his older brother to America ahead of them.
Jensen was only nine.
Imagine being that young, leaving your parents behind, travelling to another country, and trying to find your place in a world you barely understand.
But things became even more difficult.
His uncle wanted the boys to receive a good education, so he enrolled them in a boarding school in Kentucky.
There was just one problem.
It wasn't the kind of school he thought it was.
The school was actually a religious reform school for troubled teenagers.
Jensen was one of the youngest students there. He struggled with English, had a strong accent, and was one of the few Asian children.
Some of the older students were violent. His roommate was 17 and had scars from being stabbed.
And what was Jensen's daily responsibility?
Cleaning toilets.
Every single day.
But something interesting happened.
His roommate couldn't read, while Jensen could.
So they made a deal.
Jensen would teach him how to read, and in return, the older boy would teach him how to become stronger.
They became friends.
Think about that for a moment.
A nine-year-old boy, thousands of miles away from his parents, found a way to survive by identifying what someone else needed and offering something in return.
Years later, Jensen and his wife would donate $2 million to that same school to help build a dormitory and classroom building for girls.
He didn't forget where he came from.
When his parents eventually joined him in America, the family settled in Oregon.
Jensen attended Aloha High School, skipped two grades, and graduated at just 16.
He was interested in mathematics, computers, and engineering.
But he also needed money.
At 15, he got a job at Denny's, an American restaurant chain.
He started as a dishwasher.
Then he became a busboy, clearing tables, and eventually a waiter.
He worked overnight shifts while going to school.
Years later, he would say that the job helped him overcome his shyness and taught him how to work under pressure.
Interestingly, those restaurant jobs are still part of his professional story.
But nobody working alongside that teenager could have imagined what he would eventually build.
Jensen went on to study electrical engineering at Oregon State University.
After graduating, he worked as a chip designer at AMD and later joined LSI Logic.
He also attended Stanford at night, eventually earning a master's degree in electrical engineering.
By his late twenties, he had a stable career and a comfortable future.
He could have stayed there.
But he didn't.
In 1993, three engineers walked into a Denny's restaurant in San Jose, California.
Their names were Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem.
They sat in a booth, drank cheap coffee, and discussed an idea.
They wanted to build computer chips that would make video games look better.
That was the original idea behind NVIDIA.
Not artificial intelligence.
Not ChatGPT.
Not the technology powering the world's biggest data centres.
Just better graphics for video games.
They believed computers would eventually need special chips to handle increasingly realistic graphics.
Many people weren't convinced.
But the three founders took the risk.
They raised money, hired engineers, and started building.
Then came their first major mistake.
Their first graphics chip, the NV1, used a different approach from what most of the industry was adopting.
It was an intelligent idea on paper, but the rest of the industry was moving in another direction.
Game developers were building around triangles, while NVIDIA had chosen curved surfaces.
The result?
Their chip struggled to work with the software developers were already using.
Sales were disappointing.
The next product was also built around the same flawed approach.
Money started disappearing.
And the company was running out of time.
At one point, NVIDIA was roughly 30 days away from going out of business.
Let that sink in.
The company that would eventually become a multi-trillion-dollar business was once struggling to survive another month.
Jensen had a difficult decision to make.
He could continue pretending everything was fine, or admit that the technology they had built wasn't going to work.
He chose to admit the mistake.
But there was another problem.
NVIDIA had a contract with Sega, the Japanese video game company.
Jensen knew they couldn't deliver the product as originally promised.
So he travelled to Japan to meet a Sega executive named Shoichiro Irimajiri.
He explained the situation honestly.
He told him that NVIDIA couldn't deliver the chip in the way they had planned.
Then he made an unusual request.
He asked Sega to pay the remaining $5 million anyway.
Not because NVIDIA had delivered everything perfectly, but because the company needed the money to survive.
Sega could have walked away.
Instead, the executive agreed.
That $5 million gave NVIDIA the time it desperately needed.
Think about it.
Sometimes, the difference between a business that survives and one that disappears isn't a perfect business plan.
Sometimes, it's one person willing to trust you when you have very little left to offer.
But the money wasn't enough on its own.
NVIDIA had to change direction.
The company abandoned its original graphics approach and focused on the technology the wider industry was adopting.
It developed the RIVA 128 graphics chip.
The product was a success.
NVIDIA reportedly sold around a million units within its first four months.
The company that had nearly disappeared was back in the game.
In 1999, NVIDIA went public.
That same year, it introduced the GeForce 256 and helped establish the term GPU, short for Graphics Processing Unit.
At the time, these chips were mainly associated with gaming.
But Jensen noticed something other people were overlooking.
Scientists and researchers were beginning to use graphics chips for work that had nothing to do with video games.
And that observation would lead to the biggest decision in NVIDIA's history.
In 2006, NVIDIA introduced CUDA.
To understand why this mattered, imagine two kitchens.
The first has one extremely talented chef who can prepare almost any meal, but can only prepare one dish at a time.
The second has thousands of cooks, each handling a small part of the work at the same time.
The first kitchen is similar to a CPU.
The second is similar to a GPU.
A GPU can perform thousands of smaller calculations at once.
This makes it incredibly useful for certain types of scientific research, simulations, and artificial intelligence.
But there was a problem.
Using graphics chips for these other tasks was difficult.
So NVIDIA created CUDA, a system that allowed developers to write software that could use the power of its GPUs for much more than graphics.
Here is where Jensen made another unpopular decision.
He didn't reserve this technology for expensive, specialised chips.
He invested in making it available across NVIDIA's product range, including gaming graphics cards.
It cost money.
Investors questioned the decision.
For years, the investment affected profits, and many people wondered why a company known for gaming was spending so much on software that most of its customers barely used.
Jensen continued anyway.
NVIDIA made the tools available, supported universities, and helped train developers to use them.
He was building something that might not pay off immediately.
And that is what makes this decision so important.
He wasn't just selling computer chips anymore.
He was building an entire ecosystem around them.
Years later, researchers at the University of Toronto used two NVIDIA gaming graphics cards to train a system called AlexNet.
In 2012, that system achieved a remarkable result in a major image-recognition competition.
It showed the research world just how powerful GPUs could be for deep learning.
Suddenly, the same type of chips people bought to play video games could help computers learn to recognise images.
NVIDIA had spent years preparing for a market that was only beginning to emerge.
And it wasn't finished.
In 2016, Jensen personally delivered NVIDIA's first DGX-1 supercomputer to a young research organisation called OpenAI.
At the time, very few people understood just how important artificial intelligence would become.
Then came November 2022.
OpenAI released ChatGPT.
Millions of people started interacting with AI in a completely new way.
Businesses wanted their own AI systems.
Researchers wanted more computing power.
Technology companies began building enormous data centres.
And almost everyone needed the same thing:
NVIDIA's chips.
The H100 became one of the most sought-after pieces of technology in the world.
The company that started by making graphics cards for video games had become central to the artificial intelligence revolution.
Its market value climbed from $1 trillion in 2023 to $2 trillion, then $3 trillion, and eventually reached $5 trillion in 2025.
Jensen became a global celebrity.
The black leather jacket became his signature.
World leaders wanted meetings with him. People lined up for pictures and autographs.

By: Selina Nyarko Prah (Sis.)
Pastor Joseph Owusu-Boateng, Resident Minister of PIWC Winneba, has urged Christians to develop a genuine concern for the glory of God, emphasising that believers must be willing to defend His name, uphold His honour and place His purposes above their personal interests. Delivering a sermon titled “Concerns for the Glory of God” during the climax of the District Week, dubbed Grace Convocation, at PIWC Winneba, Pastor Owusu-Boateng explained that a defining characteristic of people who walk closely with God is their concern for His glory.

Drawing from 2 Samuel 7:1–4, he examined the lives of three biblical figures, David, Elijah and Nehemiah, whose devotion to God was reflected in their commitment to His honour and purposes. He began with the story of David, who, despite living in a magnificent palace, became concerned that the Ark of God remained in a tent. According to the Resident Minister, David's desire to build a house for God demonstrated a heart that placed God's glory above personal comfort.

Although David was not permitted to build the temple, he did not abandon his concern for God's house. Instead, he deliberately made extensive preparations and provided resources for its construction. Pastor Owusu-Boateng explained that David's response revealed the depth of his commitment to God. 

He challenged the congregation to consider how they would react if someone rejected an offer they had made with good intentions. He observed that many people would simply withdraw their support after such a response. David, however, continued making provisions for the temple, ensuring that the resources needed for its construction would be available.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng emphasised that genuine concern for God's glory does not disappear when personal expectations are not met. Rather, it motivates believers to remain committed to God's purposes even when they are not the ones chosen to carry out a particular assignment. He further referred to 1 Samuel 17:26, where David questioned the audacity of Goliath, the uncircumcised Philistine, who had defied the armies of the living God.

According to Pastor Owusu-Boateng, David's response was motivated by his concern for God's reputation rather than a desire for personal recognition. While others saw Goliath as a terrifying opponent, David recognised that the honour of the living God was being challenged. His willingness to confront the Philistine demonstrated a determination to defend God's name when others were afraid to act.

Turning to the life of Elijah, Pastor Owusu-Boateng referred to 1 Kings 18:21, where the prophet confronted the Israelites over their divided allegiance between God and Baal. He explained that Elijah could not tolerate the people's continued wavering between two opinions. The prophet was determined to demonstrate that the Lord alone was worthy of their worship.

Referring also to 1 Kings 18:24, he highlighted Elijah's challenge on Mount Carmel, where the God who answered by fire would be acknowledged as the true God. Pastor Owusu-Boateng explained that Elijah's actions were not intended to promote himself but to restore the people's recognition of God's supremacy. He emphasised that when a believer's motives are genuinely directed towards God's glory, God is able to demonstrate His power in defence of His name.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng also identified Nehemiah among the biblical examples of individuals whose lives reflected a deep concern for God's honour and purposes.

Drawing lessons from these examples, Pastor Owusu-Boateng outlined the characteristics of people who are genuinely concerned about the glory of God. First, he explained that such individuals are grieved whenever God is dishonoured. They do not remain indifferent when God's name is treated with contempt or when conduct within the Church brings dishonour to Him.

He further stressed that believers who genuinely love God's glory do not celebrate the failures of the Church. According to him, rather than laughing when the Church experiences difficulties or setbacks, they are moved with concern and seek its restoration and progress. He challenged Christians to examine their reactions when they hear negative reports about the Church, explaining that their responses often reveal whether their concern is for God's glory or their personal interests.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng also emphasised that people who seek God's glory live for His pleasure rather than their own. Referring to 1 Corinthians 10:31, he reminded the congregation that whether Christians eat, drink or engage in any other activity, everything should be done to the glory of God. He explained that genuine devotion to God must influence everyday decisions, personal conduct and the motives behind one's actions.

Another characteristic he highlighted was the willingness to defend the name of the Lord. He explained that believers who are concerned about God's glory do not remain silent when His name is dishonoured. Like David and Elijah, they are willing to take a stand for God even when others are unwilling to do so.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng further emphasised the responsibility of Christians to proclaim God's name and make Him known to others. He noted that concern for God's glory should not remain a private conviction but must find expression in a believer's willingness to speak about God and make His greatness known.

Pastor Owusu-Boateng explained that genuine concern for God's glory also purifies a person's motives and transforms their mindset. According to him, when God's honour becomes the primary motivation behind a believer's actions, personal ambition and the desire for recognition begin to give way to a sincere commitment to pleasing Him.

He encouraged Christians to evaluate the reasons behind their service, sacrifices and involvement in church activities, emphasising that the desire to glorify God must remain central. He further noted that those who consistently seek God's glory develop a relationship with Him marked by His favour and approval.

Concluding his message, Pastor Owusu-Boateng challenged the congregation to follow the examples of David and Elijah by demonstrating a genuine concern for God's honour in every area of life. His message reinforced the need for Christians to move beyond merely professing love for God and demonstrate that love through their willingness to defend His name, support His work, proclaim His greatness and live according to His purposes.
